To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT for Achieng’s review — Brian’s Monday Embakasi brief, 30 November

Brian,

Thank you for taking this on. Six years working together, and I know you won’t need a speech from me. What you do need is a straight account, clear limits on what we can promise, and a plan if the loading doesn’t happen. This is for you to read on Sunday, not something to circulate to the guys as it stands.

Our starting point: this is our mess, not theirs. They worked, they were due their money on Friday, and we failed to pay them. Go in with that, not with the procedure.

What happened to Friday’s pay

The bank rejected the whole payment file at 1:52pm on Friday. Its system had changed on 25 November and required a new template. The beneficiary-reference field in our file exceeded the new limit. None of the 212 payments in that file was processed.

The rejection alert went to the old finance mailbox. Kevin only saw it after 5pm, by which time the bank cut-off had passed. So this wasn’t money sitting in individual workers’ accounts waiting to clear. The file never went through.

Kevin proposed switching the payments to M-Pesa bulk. Njeri approved that on Saturday morning. She also approved KES 500 for lunch and fare for every casual on the affected list, to go in the same M-Pesa batch. The company covers the M-Pesa charges; they must not be deducted from anyone’s pay.

That is the explanation. We don’t need to name Kevin in front of the group or make the bank the villain. The template and the missed alert were ours to manage.

When the money is expected

Kevin’s current estimate is Monday by 11am. That is an estimate, not a confirmed payment time. Approval to use M-Pesa is in place; we do not yet have confirmation that the batch has been released or that everyone can receive it.

Peninah has confirmed 198 numbers. She could not reach 14 people, mostly from the Athi River intake. She’ll be at Embakasi from 7:30 with the list so they can check their numbers face to face. She is also bringing her laptop for anyone who wants a printed payslip.

Do not say “everyone will have it by 11.” In particular, we cannot give the 14 a receipt time before their details are checked and Finance confirms how their payments will be handled.

We both remember Mombasa in 2024: “by lunch” became 4pm, and half the shift sat down. No repeat of that. We can promise an update at a time we control. We cannot promise a payment time we don’t.

Before Monday’s shift

Please use Sunday to get a fresh status from Kevin: whether the M-Pesa arrangements are ready, whether 11am still holds as his estimate, what the release depends on, and how he will handle any numbers corrected after 7:30. Ask whether the 198 verified numbers can proceed without waiting for the remaining 14; don’t assume either way.

We also need a named HR contact to work with you on Monday once I’m boarding. Please agree that cover with me on Sunday. Peninah is there for payroll checks, but that does not automatically make her the HR decision-maker for a stoppage.

I’m up from 4:30 Monday. WhatsApp me before I board if anything changes, especially the payment estimate or the position on loading. My flight leaves at 7:05, so don’t count on reaching me at 7 or being able to keep me on the phone after that. Let’s have the handover sorted before then.

At the depot

5:30 — Catch Joseph first. Find out what has actually been said overnight and who is there. No arguing with people about rumours and no asking Joseph to make another “tomorrow” promise.

Before the group gathers, speak to Ouma privately. He’s loud, but he’s not a bad man. He has four children and rent to find. That’s a reminder for us to listen, not something to bring up in front of others or use to persuade him.

Something like:

“Ouma, I wanted to speak to you first. You worked and we didn’t pay you when we should have. I’m sorry. I know another promise won’t settle this. Let me tell you what is confirmed and what is still an estimate, then I want to hear what you and the others need me to understand.”

Let him finish. Don’t make getting his agreement a condition of explaining things to everyone else.

Around 6 — Speak to the whole group yourself. Njeri specifically asked for an in-person management apology. Keep it plain:

“Morning, everyone. I owe you an apology on behalf of management. Your Friday pay did not go through. Our bank file was rejected because it did not meet the new format, and we picked up the rejection too late to correct it before cut-off. You did nothing wrong.

“We are arranging payment through M-Pesa instead. Finance’s current estimate is by 11am today, but I will not tell you that is guaranteed when I cannot guarantee it. Everyone on the affected list will also receive KES 500 for Monday lunch and fare in the same batch. The company is paying the M-Pesa charges.

“Peninah will be here at 7:30 to check the numbers we haven’t been able to confirm and help with individual pay questions. I will give you another update at 8, even if the position has not changed.”

Then ask them to load the trucks. It is a request to keep the operation moving while we put this right, not a condition for receiving wages or the KES 500.

What you can and cannot promise

You can confirm the approved payment route, the KES 500 for everyone on the affected list, company-paid charges, Peninah’s attendance, and your next update.

You cannot guarantee 11am, promise an earlier payment, invent an emergency cash arrangement, or offer further compensation without approval. Don’t describe the KES 500 as settling anyone’s complaint.

Keep individual numbers and pay details off the public discussion. Let Peninah check them privately. If someone remains unpaid after others receive theirs, they need a specific follow-up with Payroll and Finance, not “everyone has been paid.”

If Ouma’s group refuses to load

The Kisumu trucks must depart by 9am to make the mill’s offloading slot. The payment estimate is two hours later. We cannot plan on the money arriving first and solving the loading problem.

If they refuse, ask calmly what they are asking for and whether anyone is willing to continue. Don’t turn it into a public contest with Ouma, and don’t pressure people to single out colleagues.

Bring in the agreed HR contact immediately. The procedure requires Operations and HR to handle any stoppage together. You can manage the immediate safety and dispatch situation, but do not make a unilateral disciplinary decision.

No dismissal, dismissal threats, or “you won’t get another contract” talk on Monday. Make that clear to Joseph and the other supervisors too. Record what happened factually: times, the concern raised, work affected, who was consulted and the response. No labels such as “troublemakers.”

At 5:30, establish with Joseph the latest safe loading start that would still allow a 9am departure. If that point is at risk, escalate to the dispatch team and Njeri then, not at 9. Ask them to work on the mill/offloading contingency. Any alternative staffing must be authorised, safe and properly qualified; no rushed loading or confrontations to save the slot. If departure cannot be met safely, report that plainly.

The procedure says grievances go first to the supervisor, then to HR within 48 hours, and that stoppages are not a grievance channel. That is our framework, not your opening speech. We already know the pay complaint and should act on it now, not send people back to start a process.

Keep the 8am update even if all you can honestly say is that you are still waiting for confirmation. Set the next update before leaving them. And when Finance says a batch has been sent, distinguish that from confirmation that each person has received their money.

Thanks, Brian. Be direct, listen, and don’t defend what we got wrong. I’ll review this tonight before we settle the Sunday checks.

Achieng
